title: Por vs Para: The Clear Guide With Examples
seo_title: Por vs Para: The Clear Guide With Examples
meta_description: Por vs para made simple: para looks ahead to a goal, por looks back at a cause or route. Clear rules, real examples, common mistakes and a quick quiz.
excerpt: Para points to a goal; por points to a cause or a path. Here is how to choose every time.

body_html:
Por vs para is the most famous preposition problem in Spanish, because English often uses one word, “for”, where Spanish needs two. The idea that solves most cases: para looks forward, toward a goal, a destination, a deadline or a person who receives something. Por looks back or through: the cause, the route, the exchange, the duration. Estudio para ser médico (I study to become a doctor) points to a goal; Lo hice por ti (I did it because of you) points to a reason.

Quick answer
  • Para = goal, purpose, destination, deadline, recipient, opinion: para mí, para el lunes.
  • Por = cause, exchange, route, duration, means, “per”: por la mañana, por teléfono.
  • Test: “in order to” or “headed to” means para; “because of”, “through” or “in exchange for” means por.
{{toc}}

Por vs para: the core idea

ParaPor
DirectionForward, toward an end pointBack to a cause, or through a path
Typical Englishin order to, for (someone), by (a deadline), towardbecause of, through, along, per, in exchange for, by (means)
ExampleSalgo para Monterrey. I’m leaving for Monterrey.Paso por Monterrey. I’m passing through Monterrey.

Think of an arrow. With para, you are standing at the start and pointing at the target. With por, you are looking at what pushed you, or at the road you traveled on.

When to use para

  • Purpose, with an infinitive: Ahorro para comprar un carro. I’m saving to buy a car.
  • Destination: Mañana salimos para Cancún. Tomorrow we leave for Cancún.
  • Recipient: Este regalo es para tu mamá. This gift is for your mom.
  • Deadline: Necesito el informe para el viernes. I need the report by Friday.
  • Opinion: Para mí, es la mejor película del año. For me, it’s the best movie of the year.
  • Comparison with what is expected: Para ser niño, habla muy bien. For a child, he speaks very well.
  • Employment: Trabajo para una empresa de software. I work for a software company.
{{image:2}}

When to use por

  • Cause or reason: Cancelaron el partido por la lluvia. They canceled the game because of the rain.
  • Exchange or price: Lo compré por 200 pesos. I bought it for 200 pesos. Gracias por todo. Thanks for everything.
  • Route or movement through: Caminamos por el parque. We walked through the park.
  • Duration: Viví en Guadalajara por dos años. I lived in Guadalajara for two years. (Spain often drops por here: viví dos años.)
  • Means of communication or transport: Hablamos por teléfono. Lo mandé por correo.
  • Parts of the day: por la mañana, por la tarde, por la noche.
  • “Per” and rates: 100 kilómetros por hora, dos veces por semana.
  • On behalf of, or instead of: ¿Puedes firmar por mí? Can you sign for me (in my place)?

Same sentence, different meaning

Some of the clearest examples come from pairs where both prepositions are possible and the meaning changes.

  • Lo hice para ti. I made it for you (as a gift). / Lo hice por ti. I did it because of you, or on your behalf.
  • Trabajo para mi papá. My dad is my boss. / Trabajo por mi papá. I’m covering my dad’s shift.
  • Salió para la tienda. She left for the store. / Pasó por la tienda. She stopped by the store.
  • Estudia para el examen. He’s studying for the exam (goal). / Aprobó por estudiar mucho. He passed because he studied a lot (cause).
{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Fixed expressions with por

Many everyday expressions simply use por, and it is easiest to learn them as whole chunks:

  • por favor (please), por fin (finally), por supuesto (of course)
  • por eso (that’s why), por ejemplo (for example), por lo menos (at least)
  • por si acaso (just in case), por cierto (by the way), por lo general (generally)

Two fixed expressions use para: para siempre (forever) and para nada (not at all).

Common por vs para mistakes

  • Gracias para la cena. Thanks is an exchange: Gracias por la cena.
  • Estudio por ser enfermera. Becoming a nurse is a goal: Estudio para ser enfermera.
  • Te llamo para la tarde. Parts of the day use por: Te llamo por la tarde.
  • Pagué 50 dólares para los boletos. Price is an exchange: Pagué 50 dólares por los boletos.

The {{link:spanish-preposition-mistakes|Spanish preposition mistakes}} guide covers other prepositions that trip learners up, such as pensar en and depender de. The Real Academia Española lists the uses of both words in its Diccionario panhispánico de dudas.

{{image:3}}

A translator’s shortcut

In my translation work, por vs para comes up in almost every document. When I hesitate between the two in a translation, I ask one question: is this sentence about where something is going, or about where it came from? Goals, destinations, deadlines and recipients are all “going”. Causes, payments, routes and durations are all “coming from” or “passing through”. That single question settles nearly every real case.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Por vs para will feel tricky for a while, and that is normal. Start with the arrow: para points ahead, por looks back or through. Learn the fixed expressions as chunks, take the quiz again next week, and you will find yourself choosing correctly without thinking. For every other pair that causes the same kind of hesitation, see my complete list of {{link:spanish-confusing-words|Spanish confusing words}}.

faq.q: What is the difference between por and para?
faq.a: Para points to a goal, destination, deadline or recipient. Por points to a cause, exchange, route, duration or means.
Always gracias por, because thanks is given in exchange for something.

faq.q: How do I say “for two years” in Spanish?
faq.a: In Latin America, por dos años is common. In Spain, people usually just say durante dos años or dos años.

faq.q: Is there an easy trick for por vs para?
faq.a: Ask whether the sentence is about where something is going (para) or where it came from or passed through (por).
